The traditional distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP) assumes that operations of a job cannot be transferred between different factories. However, in real-world production settings, the operations of a job may need to be processed in different factories owing to requirements of economic globalization or complexity of the job. Hence, in this paper, we propose a distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem with transfers (DFJSPT), in which operations of a job can be processed in different factories. An efficient memetic algorithm (EMA) is proposed to solve the DFJSPT with the objectives of minimizing the makespan, maximum workload, and total energy consumption of factories. In the proposed EMA, a well-designed chromosome presentation and initialization methods are presented to obtain a high-quality initial population. Several crossover and mutation operators and three effective neighborhood structures are designed to expand the search space and accelerate the convergence speed of the solution. Forty benchmark instances of the DFJSPT are constructed to evaluate the EMA and facilitate further studies. The Taguchi method of design of experiments is used to obtain the best combination of key EMA parameters. Extensive computational experiments are carried out to compare the EMA with three well-known algorithms from the literature. The computational results show that the EMA can obtain better solutions for approximately 90% of the tested benchmark instances compared to the three well known algorithms, thereby demonstrating the DFJSPT’s competitive performance and efficiency.

1. Introduction

Flexible job shop scheduling (FJSP) has been widely studied in recent decades (Burdett, Corry, Yarlagadda, Eustace, & Smith, 2019; Burdett & Kozan, 2018; Deliktas, Torkul, & Ustun, 2019; Deng, et al., 2017; Gong, Chiong, Deng, & Gong, 2019). In FJSP, all jobs are assumed to be processed in only one location (Al Aqel, Li, & Gao, 2019; Deng, et al., 2017; Wang, Jiang, Wang, Zhang, & Wang, 2018). However, in real-world manufacturing, products are normally processed in different factories, which are often distributed in different regions because cooperative production with different factories has obvious advantages in terms of response speed and production cost (Imen Chaouch, Driss, & Ghedira, 2019; Pan, Gao, Wang, Liang, & Li, 2019; Ying & Lin, 2018). Therefore, the distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP), in which jobs can be processed in different factories, has attracted increasingly more attention of researchers in the past decade (Chang & Liu, 2017; Iman Chaouch, Driss, & Ghedira, 2017).

The DFJSP addresses production scheduling problems existing in distributed manufacturing environments, wherein jobs are processed collaboratively by a number of flexible manufacturing units (FMUs) (De Giovanni & Pezzella, 2010; Jeong & Yim, 2009). An FMU consists of a number of enterprises (or production units); each enterprise includes several machines with different process quantities or performances (Liu, Chen, & Chou, 2014). The DFJSP is required to arrange the jobs to be processed in these enterprises, meeting objectives, such as minimizing the makespan, total machine workload, and total energy consumption. (Li, Duan, Cao, Lin, & Han, 2018; Marzouki, Driss, & Ghedira, 2018). The DFJSP has three sub-problems, which are as follows: (1) factory assignment, i.e., selecting a factory for each operation; (2) machine assignment, i.e., selecting a machine to process each operation; and (3) operation sequencing, i.e., sequencing the operations, obeying the constraints of factories, machines, and job processes simultaneously.

To date, only a limited number of researchers have studied the DFJSP. For example, Giovanni and Pezzella proposed an improved genetic algorithm (GA) to solve the DFJSP, in which an ingenious chromosome encoding and a local search strategy were integrated (De Giovanni & Pezzella, 2010). Chang and Liu presented a hybrid GA for the DFJSP with a novel encoding mechanism, and a few effective crossover and mutation operators (Chang & Liu, 2017). Liu, Chen, and Chou proposed an improved GA to solve the DFJSP, in which a refined encoding operator was designed to guarantee the diversity of chromosomes (Liu, et al., 2014). Marzouki, Driss and Ghedira proposed a chemical reaction meta-heuristic optimization method to solve the DFJSP with the objective of minimizing the makespan (Marzouki, et al., 2018). Based on a constructive procedure, Ziaee developed a fast heuristic algorithm to solve the DFJSP very quickly (Ziaee, 2013). Lu et al. developed an improved GA for the DFJSP, in which a novel concise chromosome representation was designed (Lu, Wu, Tan, Peng, & Chen, 2015). Li et al. constructed a hybrid Pareto-based tabu search algorithm to handle the DFJSP with the objectives of minimizing the makespan, maximum workload, total workload, and earliness/tardiness (Li, et al., 2018).

From the above, we can make the following observations: all the studies on the DFJSPs assumed that the jobs could not be transferred among different factories, i.e., operations of a job must be processed in the same factory; however, in real-world production systems, certain jobs may have to be processed in different factories because of reasons, such as complexity of operations or economic globalization. In addition, under energy-saving era, most of researchers focused on single objective (makespan) in DFJSP, which led to the production managers focused on economic indicator but ignored other important factors, such as energy consumption generated by processing and transferring jobs.

Inspired by these findings, in this study, we propose a distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem with transfers (DFJSPT), in which the jobs can be transferred among factories. The memetic algorithms (MAs), which hybridize evolutionary algorithms with local search (Burdett & Kozan, 2014; Chiong, Weise, & Michalewicz, 2012; Gong, et al., 2019; Kannan & Ramaraj, 2010), have delivered promising performance for solving multi-objective FJSPs (Frutos, Olivera, & Tohmé, 2010; Gong, Deng, Gong, Liu, & Ren, 2018; Wenchao, Xinyu, & Baolin, 2016; Yuan & Xu, 2013; Yuan & Xu, 2015). Motivated by their work and based on the fact that it’s hard or even impossible to obtain the optimal solutions in the acceptable time for the NP-hard problems (eg., FJSP (Gong, et al., 2020), DFJSP (De Giovanni & Pezzella, 2010), and our DFJSPT) by using mixed integer programming approaches, we present an effective memetic algorithm (EMA) to solve our proposed DFJSPT with the objectives of minimizing the makespan, maximum workload of factories, and total energy consumption. In the EMA, an effective initialization method that combines global, local, and random selections, and a crossover operator are used to obtain a highquality initial population and improve the solution diversity. In addition, a well-designed local search operator (LSO) is proposed and integrated into the EMA to improve its convergence speed and fully exploit its solution space. In addition, 40 benchmark instances are constructed to test the EMA’s performance and facilitate our future study. Finally, a suitable combination of key parameters in the EMA, which includes population size (POP\_size), crossover rate (CR\_rate), mutation rate (MU\_rate), and local search rate (LS\_rate) is obtained by using the Taguchi method of Design of Experiments (DOE) (Montgomery, 2008). Extensive experiments carried out on these 40 instances confirm the superior performance of the EMA compared to the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) (Deb, Pratap, Agarwal, & Meyarivan, 2002), non-dominated neighbor immune algorithm (NNIA) (Gong, Jiao, Du, & Bo, 2008) and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm III (NSGA-III) (Deb & Jain, 2014).

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, a mathematical model of the DFJSPT is presented. In Section 3, the EMA is described in detail. The numerical experiments and discussions are presented in Section 4. Finally, we draw some conclusions and describe the future work in Section 5.
2. Model description and example
2.1. Problem description and mathematical mode

The DFJSPT consists of J jobs assignments $\left\{ J _ { 1 } , J _ { 2 } , \ldots , J _ { I } \right\}$ , which need to be processed in F factories $\{ F _ { 1 } , F _ { 2 } , \dots , F _ { F } \}$ , and these factories are geographically distributed in several regions. Each job has several operations $\{ O _ { j 1 } , O _ { j 2 } , \dots , O _ { j O l j } \}$ , and each of these operations must be processed, one after the other on a machine from among the available machines from F factories, after satisfying the respective precedence constraint. The processing time and unit energy consumption of each machine for operation $O _ { j o }$ are ascertained in advance. Three objectives, including makespan, maximum workload of factories, and total energy consumption, are considered in this model. The tasks of the DFJSPT are generalized as follows:
(1) Determine how to assign each operation of the J jobs to F factories.
(2) Assign a machine to each operation.
(3) Sequence the operations of the J jobs.

The assumptions made in this model are as follows:

3. Memetic algorithm for DFJSPT
3.1. Brief introduction to NSGA-II

The NSGA-II, which is an effective evolutionary algorithm for multi-objective scheduling problem, has been extensively used over the past decades. Two major theories of NSGA-II, which are non-dominated sorting and crowding distance computing, are used by many multi-objective algorithms for their unique advan-

tages in choosing good individuals. The non-dominated sorting operator is used to evaluate the quality of individuals by distinguishing the dominant relationship between individuals, and the crowding distance is used to enhance the diversity of the solutions and to obtain a uniform non-dominated solution set. The main steps of NSGA-II are described as follows. Firstly, the parent and offspring population of generation t with the same size N, i.e., $P _ { t }$ and C, respectively are defined. Next, a new population $R _ { t }$ is obtained by combining P and $C _ { t } , \mathrm { i . e . , } R _ { t } = P _ { t } \cup C _ { t }$ . Then, an operator <sup>[</sup>termed ‘‘non-dominated sorting”, is implemented to distinguish the non-dominated levels in population R<sub>t</sub>. Individuals of the next generation $P _ { t + 1 }$ (of size N) are selected according to the ranking results. It should be noted that another operator ‘‘crowding distance computing” is used as a reference to select the individuals when the same rank appears in $R _ { t } ,$ and an individual with a larger crowding distance will be assigned to $P _ { t + 1 }$ . More details about NSGA-II can be obtained in Deb, Pratap, Agarwal, and Meyarivan (2002).

text: 3.2.4. Crossover operator

In the crossover operator, only a multiple operation crossover (MOX) for the OS vector is designed, because not all of the machines can handle every operation. The aim of MOX is to increase the population diversity by a crossover on an operation sequence. The key steps of MOX are described below, in which $P _ { 1 }$ and $P _ { 2 }$ are defined as two parents, and $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ are the offspring. Assume that $P _ { 1 }$ and $P _ { 2 }$ have been produced and are as shown in Fig. 4. The offspring $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ are generated from the following steps:
Step 1: randomly generate two positions on the OS vector, marked Position 1 and Position 2. As shown in Fig. 4, Positions 1 and 2 are 4 and 9, respectively.

Step 2: find the gene fragments between Positions 1 and 2 in $P _ { 1 } ,$ which is [3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2]; find the gene fragment between Positions 1 and 2 in $P _ { 2 } ,$ which is [2, 1, 4, 3, 4, 3]. Note that the operations in the two gene fragments are determined again according to the chromosome encoding, for example, [3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2] corresponds to $[ O _ { 3 1 } , O _ { 2 1 } , O _ { 1 1 } , O _ { 1 2 } , O _ { 1 3 } , O _ { 2 2 } ] .$

Step 3: find all the positions in $P _ { 2 }$ with the same information as [3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2] from the left to the right; the positions found in $P _ { 2 }$ are the first, third, fifth, seventh, tenth, and twelfth.

Step 4: insert the genes of [3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2] in $P _ { 1 }$ to the first, third, fifth, seventh, tenth, and twelfth positions of $C _ { 1 }$ from the left to the right; insert the genes of $P _ { 2 } ,$ except those in the first, third, fifth, seventh, tenth, and twelfth positions, into $C _ { 1 }$ from the left to the right.

3.2.5. Mutation operator

A population generated by the GLR method may be a partial optimal solution, because the machines with the longest processing time may be assigned to some operations during the process of balancing the makespan and workload of the factories. To avoid this problem, we propose an ‘‘inversing sequencing mutation” (ISM) of three successive genes on the OS vector, and a ‘‘replacing machine mutation” (RMM) of the two positions on the MA vector. The ISM reduces the three objectives by optimizing the sequence of operations, while the RMM reduces the processing time and transfer time by changing the processing machines of the two operations. At every iteration, only either the ISM or RMM is used, i.e., if a random number from 0 to 1 is greater than 0.5, the RMM is used, and ISM is used, otherwise. To make the ISM and RMM clearer, assume that a parent individual $\mathsf { P } _ { 3 }$ has been generated. Now, the offspring C3 by the ISM and C4 by the RMM are generated from the following steps.
Firstly, offspring ${ \sf C } _ { 3 }$ is acquired by following steps:
Step 1: randomly generate two positions on the OS vector in $\mathrm { P } _ { 3 } ,$ marked Position 1 and Position 2. As shown in Fig. 5, Positions 1 and 2 are 3 and 5, respectively.

3.2.6. Local search operator (LSO)

In this section, an LSO is proposed to accelerate the convergence speed and expand the solution space of the EMA. Many previous studies, such as Yuan and Xu (2015) and Wang, Zhou, Xu, Wang, and Liu (2012), demonstrated that the makespan for a predetermined scheduling could be minimized only by moving the operations on the critical path (also called the critical operations path). Hence, taking inspiration from the aforementioned studies, here, we design three methods for the LSO. The first method swaps two positions of the critical operations (LSO\_SP) based on critical blocks (Li, Pan, & Liang, 2010). The second method converts the current factory and machine to other alternatives with a minimum processing time (LSO\_MPT). The third method replaces the current factory and machine with other alternatives that can reduce the transfer time to the maximum extent possible (LSO\_RTT). The core pseudo code of the LSO is shown in Algorithm 2, while two other pseudo codes related to the three LSOs are given in Algorithms 3 and 4 respectively.

4. Numerical experiments and discussions

The proposed EMA for the DFJSPT was executed in MATLAB R2016 and computed on a PC equipped with an Intel<sup></sup> Core i5 3.3 GHz and 8 GB RAM processor. To eliminate extraneous solutions during the computations, 10 numerical experiments were conducted for each benchmark instance.
4.1. Construction of the DFJSPT benchmarks

To test the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed EMA, we built new benchmarks named DFMs 01–40 by extending the current popular benchmarks from the FJSP (Hurink, Jurisch, & Thole, 1994). To compare the performance of the EMA with the other previous effective multi-objective algorithms for solving the DFJSPT, DFMs 01–40 were classified as small size instances (DFMs 01– 15), middle size instances (DFMs 16–30), and large size instances (DFMs 31–40). The three types of instances were generated by setting the available factory collection, maximum machine rank, and available machine numbers in each factory as [2, 4, 6], [6, 8, 10], and [1–2, 1–3, 1–4] respectively. In addition, the transfer times of jobs were predetermined as 30 units for a job transfer between machines in the same factory and 60 units for a job transfer between different factories). The energy consumption for each job during the transfer was taken as 6 units. The instance information used in this study can be downloaded on line at https:/ github.com/hnulq191817880/mygit2019.git.

4.6. Comparison with other algorithms

To further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed EMA, we compared the same with the NNIA, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III using three experiments. The reasons for choosing those algorithms to make a comparison with EMA are as follows: (i) they have been widely used to solve multi-objective optimization problems; (ii) they use the non-dominated sorting method to deal with multiobjectives; and (iii) they are usually used as classical algorithms to evaluate the effectiveness of new algorithms with multiobjective problems (Siqueira, Freitas Souza, & Souza, 2020; Liang, et al., 2015; Ticona Gutierrez, Adamatti, & Bravo, 2019; Zhu, et al., 2019).

text: 5. Conclusions and future studies

In this study, we proposed an extended model of distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP), i.e. distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem with transfers (DFJSPT), in which jobs can be processed in multiple factories by transfers. A mathematical model of DFJSPT was constructed with the optimization objectives of makespan, maximum workload of the factories, and the total energy consumption simultaneously. An effective memetic algorithm (EMA) was developed to solve this model. The effectiveness of the EMA has been proved by a variety of experiments, and the computational results can provide the best or near best solutions with three objectives for distributed factory managers from a global perspective.

The proposed model of DFJSPT makes full use of distributed resources in many factories to obtain the overall optimal production solution. In this model, each job has several operations, and these operations can be processed in many factories. To the best of our knowledge, the traditional researches normally assume that all operations of the same job can only be processed in a factory. However, in the real production, the operations of a job may need to be processed in different factories, or more optimal scheduling solutions can be obtained if the operations of jobs can be processed in different factories considering the production resource comprehensively. Hence. We extended the existing model of DFJSP, in which each operation could be assigned to an appropriate machine in the distributed factories. Besides, under the context of globalization and saving energy, more indicators should be taken into account in the scheduling model, such as energy consumption, but the previous papers normally focused on single objective (makespan) in their model, which may consume excessive resources to complete the economic objective, and ultimately lead to waste of energy. With regards to this, we formed a multiobjective optimization model, where the makespan, workload of factories, and energy consumption were considered simultaneously. This twofold improvements of the proposed model can provide a reference for the subsequent research on DFJSP.

We proposed an EMA to solve the DFJSPT aiming at optimizing the makespan, workload of factories, and energy consumption simultaneously. In the EMA, a well-designed three levels encoding method, and some crossover and mutation operators were integrated. A specially designed GLR initialization method, which includes global (G), local (L), and random (R) selection methods, was used to obtain a high-quality initial population, and three neighborhood structures based on the critical path in the local search operator (LSO) were proposed to improve the convergence speed and fully exploit the solution space. In our experiments, a total of 40 benchmark instances of the DFJSPT were first constructed to facilitate the verification of the performance of the EMA. Next, we used the Taguchi method of DOE to obtain the best combination of key parameters in the EMA. Finally, extensive comparisons were carried out between our proposed EMA and three well-known algorithms based on the constructed benchmarks. From the comparison results, we see that the EMA outperforms other three compared algorithms more than about 90% of the tested benchmarks.

Owing to requirements of globalization, this research provided theoretical and practical significance. Theoretically, we have developed a research direction for the DFJSP and proposed an effective algorithm to solve the problem. From a practical stand point, our constructed DFJSPT model can support production managers who work in distributed manufacturing units in scheduling jobs in a manner that is in line with the actual production. If production managers could consider job transfers among distributed factories, they can produce a more feasible and efficient scheduling scheme.

As part of a future work, we plan to study the DFJSPT in more detail. For example, we shall consider the dynamic transfer time between machines, and the batch transportation of jobs between factories in distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem.
